A multi-narrator Victorian novel: six single-narrator sections (the house-steward's two chapters, the pious cousin's, the solicitor's, the cousin-suitor's two). Names renamed (see PROVENANCE.md).
author: Wilkie Collins
source: Project Gutenberg #155 (public domain, US; PG wrapper stripped)
synopsis: A great yellow diamond, the Larkstone, looted from a Hindu shrine at the storming of Kalinpur by Colonel Stannard, is left by his will to his niece Isabel Castlemere, to be given her on her eighteenth birthday at her widowed mother Lady Honoria Castlemere's country house in Coldmoor. Amos Pennock, the family's elderly house-steward, who consults a well-worn copy of Jonas Harrow in every crisis, tells how her cousin Lewis Tremayne brings the gem down, three Indians watch the house, Isabel wears the stone at her birthday dinner, where the guests include her other cousin, the philanthropist Cecil Mortlake, and it vanishes from her room overnight. The celebrated detective Sergeant Pellow suspects the troubled housemaid Dorcas Coldridge and even Isabel herself, who will no longer speak to Lewis. Later narrators take up the story: Isabel's pious, meddling cousin Miss Tabitha Sneyd records Isabel's brief engagement to Cecil and Lady Castlemere's death; the family solicitor Mr. Hedley explains the will and the diamond's pledge to the moneylender Barnaby Grisewood; and Lewis, back from abroad, finds Dorcas's hidden letter and the paint-stained nightgown that proves he himself took the stone. A re-enactment shows he did it unknowingly, under laudanum the family doctor gave him in secret. The trail leads to a London bank, from which Cecil, ruined by debt, redeems the gem and is found murdered in disguise; the Indians carry the Larkstone back to its shrine, and Lewis and Isabel marry.
